cards.a: Channels are the RF sub-bands APs transmit on. Non-overlapping channels let nearby APs share spectrum without colliding; DFS adds radar-aware channels in 5 GHz; and RRM automatically tunes channel and power.
In the 2.4 GHz band the non-overlapping channels are 1, 6, and 11 in the US. The band has channels 1-13 (US 1-11) at 20 MHz width with 5 MHz spacing.

cards.q: What are the characteristics of 5 GHz channels?
cards.a: 5 GHz offers many wider channels across the UNII bands (36-165). DFS channels 52-144 require radar detection with no radar requirement on non-DFS channels like 36, 40, 44, 48, and 149+. More channels mean less interference, but DFS needs radar detection.

cards.q: How do 20/40/80/160 MHz channel widths behave across bands?
cards.a: 20 MHz is the standard width in both 2.4 and 5 GHz; 40 MHz bonds channels in both; 80/160 MHz are not used in 2.4 but give high speeds in 5 GHz. Wider channels mean more throughput but leave less spectrum available.

cards.q: What is DFS and what does it do?
cards.a: Dynamic Frequency Selection (DFS) avoids radar. An AP must listen before using a DFS channel, change channel if radar is detected (with brief downtime), and some regions limit DFS channel use.

cards.q: What is RRM and what does it automate?
cards.a: Radio Resource Management (RRM), run by the WLC, automatically assigns non-overlapping channels, adjusts transmit power via TPC, monitors client coverage, and detects interference.
TPC (Transmit Power Control) adjusts AP transmit power automatically, one of the RRM functions.

cards.q: What commands enable RRM channel and power assignment?
cards.a: ap dot11 5ghz rrm channel global and ap dot11 24ghz rrm channel global let RRM pick channels; ap dot11 5ghz rrm tx-power global enables automatic power; ch-width sets the channel width.

cards.q: What commands verify channel and radio settings?
cards.a: show ap radio summary, show ap dot11 5ghz summary, show ap dot11 24ghz summary, show ap config general, and show ap monitor channel.

cards.q: Clients see interference and slow performance. What are the likely causes and checks?
cards.a: Interference usually means overlapping channels, so check RRM channel assignment; slow performance often means co-channel APs, so check the radio summary.

cards.q: DFS stalls, low power, and busy air appear. What should you check?
cards.a: DFS stalls point to radar on the channel (check DFS status), low power points to TPC (check tx-power), and busy air points to noise (check with show ap monitor).

cards.q: Which Channels quick review facts should you remember?
cards.a: 2.4 GHz non-overlap is 1, 6, 11; 5 GHz has many channels with DFS 52-144; widths are 20/40/80/160; RRM auto-assigns channels; TPC auto-adjusts power; overlapping channels are avoided; monitor scans the air.
